name: Denisovans
hook: A new human lineage identified in 2010 from a finger bone's DNA, before any diagnostic skeleton was found.
claim: In 2010, DNA from a finger bone in Denisova Cave, Siberia, was shown to belong to a hominin distinct from Neanderthals and modern humans. Named 'Denisovans', the group was defined from molecular data alone, before any remains could be diagnosed by anatomy.

claimed_age.label: ~48,000-30,000 years (Denisova 3, by cave stratigraphy)
claimed_age.basis: Age of the finger bone (Denisova 3) as originally reported, inferred from its stratigraphic layer at Denisova Cave, not a direct date on the bone itself.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: Neanderthals were the only well-established non-modern hominin known in Late Pleistocene Eurasia; no distinct archaic Asian lineage was recognized.

unambiguous_signal.note: A complete mitochondrial genome, then a nuclear genome, matched no known human, Neanderthal or ape sequence; contamination was measured at ~0.1-0.2%, too low to explain the result.

documented_context.note: The finger bone (Denisova 3) came from an excavated layer at Denisova Cave; its age came from that layer, not a direct date on the bone. Karst deposits can be locally disturbed.

multiple_dating_methods.note: At the time of the claim, the age rested on the radiocarbon-dated stratigraphic sequence alone. Direct multi-method dating of hominin fragments followed only in 2019.

multiple_labs.note: Both 2010 papers used DNA from the same Leipzig facility; the nuclear genome was analysed by a separate group (Reich, Harvard) using independent statistical methods.

professional_recovery.note: Excavated by the long-running Russian Academy of Sciences (Siberian Branch) project at Denisova Cave, led by Derevianko, Shunkov and colleagues.

peer_reviewed_report.note: Both founding results appeared as full papers in Nature within the same year (March and December 2010).

material_accessible.note: Sequence data were deposited in public repositories, and specimens curated in Novosibirsk have since been restudied by other groups, e.g. by collagen fingerprinting of further bone fragments.

independent_teams.note: Fossil recovery and sequencing stayed within one Leipzig-centred consortium through this window; other population geneticists soon used the published genome to study living populations.

proponent_stake.note: Academic consortium (Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology; Harvard Medical School); no commercial, religious or nationalist motive documented in the sources reviewed.

objections.text: Ancient-DNA claims of deep, previously unknown lineages have often turned out to reflect modern human contamination of the sample or sequencing library rather than a real archaic population.
objections.raised_by: Standard methodological caution in the ancient-DNA field
objections.outcome_note: Krause et al. and Reich et al. measured present-day human mtDNA contamination in their libraries at about 0.1-0.2% and reproduced the signal across independent extracts and a second molecule (nuclear DNA).

objections.text: Denisovans have no formally published species name or morphological holotype; for years only a handful of fragmentary remains from a single site had been attributed to them, entirely by molecular data.
objections.outcome_note: Fossils outside Siberia (Xiahe 2019, Harbin 2025) now corroborate the lineage, but no binomial name is formally validated, and its rank as a species or a Homo erectus/heidelbergensis population is still debated.

objections.text: The Xiahe mandible was a surface find handed to researchers by a monk in 1980 with no excavation record; its ~160,000-year age comes from U-series dating of a carbonate crust on the bone, not the bone itself.
objections.outcome_note: The protein-based Denisovan identification of the mandible is not disputed, but its own age remains an inference from the adhering crust rather than a direct measurement; no subsequent direct date was found.

objections.text: Nearly every specimen defining the Denisovans passed through one research consortium, raising the question of whether the finding depended on independent replication.
objections.outcome_note: By 2019-2025, separate institutions (Lanzhou University with Copenhagen proteomics for Xiahe; the Chinese Academy of Sciences for Harbin) corroborated Denisovan identifications independently.

status_note: A genetically distinct Denisovan population is accepted throughout paleoanthropology and population genetics, corroborated at three sites using nuclear DNA, sediment DNA and ancient proteins. Debate continues only over its taxonomic rank.
what_settled_it: Independent mitochondrial and nuclear genome analyses of the same bone, published months apart in 2010, agreed it belonged to no known population and, via the nuclear genome, showed a detectable ancestry signal in living Melanesians.

timeline.event: Systematic Russian excavations at Denisova Cave, Altai, are already under way (begun c. 1979, per a 2019 retrospective).
A monk finds a hominin mandible at Baishiya Karst Cave, Xiahe, on the Tibetan Plateau, China, later called the Xiahe mandible.
A hominin finger-bone fragment, later named Denisova 3, is excavated at Denisova Cave.
Krause et al. sequence its complete mitochondrial genome and report a lineage unlike Neanderthals or modern humans.
Reich et al. sequence the nuclear genome, name the group 'Denisovans', and detect ~4-6% Denisovan ancestry in present-day Melanesians.
Slon et al. recover Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA directly from cave sediment with no skeletal remains, a method later applied at Baishiya.
Slon et al. sequence 'Denisova 11', a first-generation daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father.
Chen et al. identify the Xiahe mandible as Denisovan by ancient protein analysis, the first Denisovan fossil outside Denisova Cave.
Douka, Jacobs et al. use Bayesian-modelled radiocarbon and optical dating to show hominin occupation at Denisova Cave extends back at least 200,000 years.
Zhang et al. detect Denisovan mitochondrial DNA in Baishiya Karst Cave sediment, independently corroborating Denisovan presence there.
Ji, Wu et al. describe the Harbin cranium as a new species, 'Homo longi', with no molecular link to Denisovans.
Fu, Cao et al. recover Denisovan mitochondrial DNA from dental calculus on the Harbin cranium, linking it to the Denisovan lineage.

decisive_tests.test: Recover nuclear DNA or a proteome from additional Xiahe- or Harbin-associated skeletal material to build a second high-coverage Denisovan genome outside Denisova Cave.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the Tibetan and Northeast Asian Denisovan populations were genetically distinct from the Siberian lineage, and would support formally naming the group.

falsifier: Independent reanalysis showing the Denisova 3 sequences were contaminated or artefactual, or repeated failure to replicate Denisovan DNA or proteins in the Siberian, Tibetan or Harbin material, would overturn this status. No such failure is reported.

sources.citation: Krause, J., Fu, Q., Good, J.M., Viola, B. et al. (2010). The complete mitochondrial DNA genome of an unknown hominin from southern Siberia. Nature 464(7290): 894-897.
sources.note: Abstract read in full: mtDNA from the Denisova finger bone, excavated 2008, dated 48,000-30,000 yr by stratigraphy; lineage distinct from Neanderthal/modern human out-of-Africa migrations.

sources.citation: Reich, D., Green, R.E., Kircher, M., Krause, J. et al. (2010). Genetic history of an archaic hominin group from Denisova Cave in Siberia. Nature 468(7327): 1053-1060.
sources.note: Full introduction/results sections read: names 'Denisovans', reports ~4-6% Melanesian ancestry, discusses mtDNA-vs-nuclear divergence discrepancy, and gives contamination estimates (~0.1-0.2%).

sources.citation: Chen, F., Welker, F., Shen, C., Bailey, S.E. et al. (2019). A late Middle Pleistocene Denisovan mandible from the Tibetan Plateau. Nature 569(7756): 409-412.
sources.note: Read in full: mandible identified by ancient protein analysis at Baishiya Karst Cave, Xiahe; acknowledgements confirm it was provided by an anonymous monk; U-series dating used a carbonate crust.

sources.citation: Zhang, D., Xia, H., Chen, F., Li, B. et al. (2020). Denisovan DNA in Late Pleistocene sediments from Baishiya Karst Cave on the Tibetan Plateau. Science 370(6516): 584-587.
sources.note: Abstract read: Denisovan mitochondrial DNA recovered from Baishiya sediment, indicating presence at about 100, 60 and possibly 45 thousand years ago.

sources.citation: Fu, Q., Cao, P., Dai, Q., Bennett, E.A. et al. (2025). Denisovan mitochondrial DNA from dental calculus of the >146,000-year-old Harbin cranium. Cell 188(15): 3919-3926.e9.
sources.note: Abstract read: no DNA from tooth or petrous bone, but mtDNA from dental calculus falls within Denisovan variation, related to an early Siberian Denisovan branch.

sources.citation: Ji, Q., Wu, W., Ji, Y., Li, Q. et al. (2021). Late Middle Pleistocene Harbin cranium represents a new Homo species. The Innovation 2(3): 100132.
sources.note: Abstract read: proposes the Harbin cranium as a new Homo species based on morphology; no DNA/protein evidence and no Denisovan link in this paper.

sources.citation: Peyrégne, S., Slon, V., Kelso, J. (2024). More than a decade of genetic research on the Denisovans. Nature Reviews Genetics 25(2): 83-103.
sources.note: Abstract open, full text paywalled. Confirms only ~10 fragmentary remains from two sites attributed to Denisovans by molecular data alone as of this review.

sources.citation: Slon, V., Mafessoni, F., Vernot, B., de Filippo, C. et al. (2018). The genome of the offspring of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. Nature 561(7721): 113-116.
sources.note: Full text (PMC) read: Denisova 11 is a first-generation Neanderthal-Denisovan offspring, ~38.6% Neanderthal-like and ~42.3% Denisovan-like informative alleles.

sources.citation: Douka, K., Slon, V., Jacobs, Z., Ramsey, C.B. et al. (2019). Age estimates for hominin fossils and the onset of the Upper Palaeolithic at Denisova Cave. Nature 565(7741): 640-644.
sources.note: Abstract/intro accessible, full text paywalled: 50 radiocarbon dates plus 3 direct hominin dates, Bayesian-modelled; cites prior data deposition in ENA/GenBank.

sources.citation: Jacobs, Z., Li, B., Shunkov, M.V., Kozlikin, M.B. et al. (2019). Timing of archaic hominin occupation of Denisova Cave in southern Siberia. Nature 565(7741): 594-599.
sources.note: Abstract accessible, full text paywalled: prior chronology relied on radiocarbon (to ~50 ka) plus less reliable TL/palaeomagnetism/genetics; this paper adds 103 OSL dates.

sources.citation: Dennell, R. (2019). Dating of hominin discoveries at Denisova. Nature 565(7741): 571-572.
sources.note: Read in full (News & Views): cave occupied >=200,000 yr; excavations began ~1979; notes karst deposits can be disturbed by burrowing, subsidence and freeze-thaw.

confidence_note: Founding genetic papers and the hybrid/mandible/Harbin papers were read in full or substantial part, all open access. Two site-chronology papers and the 2023 review were only abstract-readable.
corrections: Starter notes described the 2025 Harbin attribution as via 'proteins or DNA'; it was specifically ancient mitochondrial DNA recovered from dental calculus (Fu, Cao et al. 2025), not protein.

'Denisovan' is not a formally established Linnaean species name; no binomial with a designated holotype has been validly published. It remains an informal lineage name defined by molecular (and now some morphological) evidence.
The Xiahe mandible was not a fresh 2019 discovery; it was found by a local monk in 1980 and only scientifically dated, analysed and published decades later.
notes: This record treats 2010-2025 as one case: each later specimen (Xiahe, Harbin) corroborates the 2010 claim rather than making a new one. A real puzzle: the 2010 mtDNA alone implied a split twice as deep as the Neanderthal-human split; the nuclear genome, published the same year, instead placed Denisovans as sister to Neanderthals, so the mtDNA reflected that lineage's own history, not the population's divergence time. No sustained rebuttal of the core 2010 claim was found; this looks like fast, low-resistance acceptance from convergent molecular evidence, not a contested anomaly.

open_issues: Could not confirm a revised direct date for Denisova 3; Douka et al. 2019 revised the chronology but the paywalled full text with the exact figure could not be read, so accepted_age is left null.

No Wikimedia Commons file titles for Denisova Cave, the finger bone or the Xiahe/Harbin specimens could be confirmed within budget (four guesses all 'NOT FOUND'); plates were skipped rather than guessed.

The 'independent_teams' and 'multiple_labs' features are 'partial' because founding sequencing stayed within one Leipzig-centred consortium through ~2015; skeptic should check for an earlier independent replication I may have missed.
No named critic of the core 2010 claim was found; objections 1, 2 and 4 are general methodological cautions, not attributed to specific people. Worth a second search pass with more sources.
